core: A dictionary/map/associative array is a collection of key->value pairs
Keys are unique within one dictionary and are (usually) required to be hashable/immutable
Access is BY KEY, not by integer position
Average-case O(1) lookup/insert/delete via hashing; worst-case O(n) when many keys collide
Ordering: classically unordered; Python dicts preserve insertion order (guaranteed since 3.7)
supporting: Terminology map: Python 'dictionary' = 'map'/'hash map'/'associative array' in other languages
A hash table is the usual implementation: a hash function maps keys to array positions; a collision is two keys mapping to the same slot
Common operations: insert/update by key, lookup, membership test, delete, size
One small correct worked example building and querying a dict
outOfScope: Big-O theory itself (own topic time-complexity: state complexities, do not teach the notation)
Arrays and lists in depth (own topics: contrast in one sentence — index vs key access)
Internals of specific hash functions and collision-resolution schemes beyond one sentence

claims.claim: A dictionary (associative array) is a collection of items randomly accessible by a key; it stores key->value pairs.
The keys of one dictionary must be unique, and keys must be an immutable/hashable type; dictionaries are indexed by keys rather than by a range of numbers as sequences are.
The usual implementation is a hash table: a hash function maps keys to array positions, and two keys mapping to the same position is a collision.
With a good hash function and enough table space, lookup/insert/delete run in average-case constant time O(1); with many collisions the worst case degrades to O(n).
Dictionaries are classically unordered, but Python dict objects preserve insertion order; this was an implementation detail in CPython 3.6 and became part of the language specification in Python 3.7.

Worked example (verified in python3): building {'apple':30,'banana':10,'cherry':75}, inserting 'date', updating 'apple', dict['cherry'] returns 75, .get('mango','not found') returns the default, 'banana' in d is True, len is 4, and keys iterate in insertion order.
The name differs by language: Python calls it 'dictionary'; other languages/traditions call the same structure a 'map', 'hash map', or 'associative array'.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a dictionary ordered or unordered?
positions: Abstractly, a map/associative array is an unordered collection keyed by value, not position.
Concretely, Python dicts preserve insertion order (guaranteed since 3.7); many other languages' hash maps do not.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the abstract structure as unordered-by-definition, then note the concrete Python guarantee as a language-specific property, distinguishing 'insertion order preserved' from 'sorted by key'.

sourceRecords.title: hash table — Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures (DADS)
sourceRecords.provider: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Defines a hash table as 'A dictionary in which keys are mapped to array positions by hash functions,' notes collisions when multiple keys map to one position, and states complexity 'may be constant (Theta(1)) if the table is big enough.' Supports the hashing mechanism and the average-constant-time claim.

sourceRecords.title: Data Structures — The Python Tutorial (Dictionaries, section 5.5)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. States a dictionary is 'a set of key: value pairs, with the requirement that the keys are unique (within one dictionary)' and that 'dictionaries are indexed by keys, which can be any immutable type.' Supports the key->value / uniqueness / key-not-index / immutable-key claims. Facts used; prose original.

sourceRecords.title: Built-in Types — Mapping Types (dict)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Documents dict as a mapping type whose keys must be hashable, and carries the 'Changed in version 3.7: Dictionary order is guaranteed to be insertion order' note. Supports hashable-keys and insertion-order claims.
